1:
The occasion is guessed at and the timing is not. Henry supposes some anniversary solemnity, for a birthday or a coronation or one of their idols, and reports that historians say the besieging general knew of the feast and, presuming the city would be off its guard, buried in sleep and wine, took that opportunity to attack it. Wesley says the eastern kings showed their magnificence in this way, but calls it prodigious that he should carouse when the city was besieged and ready to be taken. Ellicott finds nothing unreasonable in the number of guests, since the ancient version doubles it, and takes the drinking before the thousand to mean the king had a table reserved for himself apart from them.

Henry reads the whole feast as an affront. The city was besieged, a powerful enemy at the gates, his kingdom at stake, and in all this the hand of the Lord had gone out against him, calling him to weeping and mourning and sackcloth; but, as one resolved to walk contrary to God, he proclaims a feast instead, as if he dared the Almighty to do his worst, and spends extravagantly to show how little he feared having to surrender for want of provisions. Security and sensuality, Henry adds, are sad presages of ruin, and those who will not be warned by the judgments of God may expect to be wounded by them.

Placing the king costs Gill and Calvin arithmetic. Gill counts the intervening reigns, sets aside those who make Belshazzar the immediate successor or a younger brother, and takes him for a grandson of Nebuchadnezzar; Wesley says the same in a line; and Calvin reckons that about seventy years had passed since Daniel was led into exile, adding that the seventy of the earlier prophecy should be counted neither from that exile nor from the destruction of the city, but from the slaughter between the first victory of Nebuchadnezzar and the burning of the temple. Calvin explains the word father as the usage of all languages, which calls ancestors fathers. Clarke goes further than any of them and holds that the chapter stands out of its place and should come in after the seventh and eighth.

Why the vessels were sent for is settled by ruling out a kinder motive. Keil and Delitzsch reject an interpreter who supposed the king, anxious on account of the siege, fetched them to seek the favour of the God of the Jews: that does not harmonize with the celebration of so riotous a festival, and the vessels are not brought for libations to propitiate the God to whom they were consecrated, but, by the plain statement of the text, only to drink out of them in the madness of lust. Ellicott asks what led him to think of the God of Israel in the midst of the revelry, and allows it may have been a drunken fancy, or that he had been warned that the prophets foretold the overthrow of Babylon by the army then in the neighbourhood; but whatever the explanation, the act was defiance. Clarke puts it in a proverb, that when wine got fully in, wit went wholly out; and Gill reports a reading that personifies the wine as giving the advice.

Calvin makes the recklessness itself a judgment. When the destruction of a house is at hand the impious pull out its posts and gates, and God, when he means to execute his judgments, impels the reprobate by a secret instinct to rush forward and hasten their own destruction. Belshazzar did exactly this: his carelessness marked his stupidity and the wrath of God, since in the midst of his pride and crimes he could delight in revelling, and his blindness points out the vengeance the more clearly, since he was not content with his own intemperance but must openly declare war against God.
3:
Only the gold is named, and both Gill and Calvin think more came. Gill says the servants fetched them from the temple of Bel and brought them to the house of the king, and that though only golden vessels are mentioned, no doubt the silver were brought too, according to the command. Calvin supposes the word is used because the most precious were brought, silver being passed over while the more splendid are noticed. He observes also that the prophet does not say Nebuchadnezzar carried them off but treats it as the common act of all the Babylonians, since they obtained the victory under his direction and all were engaged in it. Keil and Delitzsch note only that the word used denotes the holy place, the inner apartment of the temple.

Calvin makes much of the phrase that names the place they came from. It is not enough to say from Jerusalem; the prophet says from the temple of the house of God, and by that he sharpens the impiety of the king and his nobles in erecting their horns against the God of Israel. There is a great contrast between the God who commanded his temple to be built there and sacrifices to be offered to him, and the gods now praised over his cups. This, Calvin says, was the head and front of the offending, that the king purposely rose up against God, and not only oppressed the Jews tyrannically but triumphed over their God, the Creator of heaven and earth; and the madness hastened his own destruction and with it the time of their deliverance.

Keil and Delitzsch explain why the drinking is mentioned twice. The clause is repeated in order to make manifest the connection between the drinking and the praising of the gods, and the wickedness lay in this, that they drank out of the holy vessels of the temple of the God of Israel in order to glorify their heathen gods in songs of praise. In doing so, they say, the company did not merely place the God of Israel on a perfect level with their own gods, as one interpreter puts it, but raised their gods above the Lord of heaven, as Daniel afterwards charges the king. They add the logic of the whole act: the carrying away of the vessels to Babylon and the placing of them in the temple of Bel was a sign of the defeat of the God to whom they had been consecrated, so that using them for wine amid songs in praise of those gods was a celebration of them as victorious over him.

What the wine contributed Calvin is careful not to overstate. He does not ascribe the praise of the false gods to drunkenness, but obliquely shows that their petulance was increased by drink: had each been sober at home he would not have risen so rashly against God, but where impiety already exists in the heart, intemperance becomes an additional stimulus. Gill supposes they drank out of the temple vessels perhaps until they were drunk, and Wesley says they were at the same time insulting the great God of heaven and earth. On the list of materials Calvin notes that the prophet names them reproachfully, since God has nothing in common with either gold or silver, and his true image cannot be expressed in corruptible stuff.
5:
Whose hand it was they answer carefully. Gill says it came from heaven, or as if out of the wall, and was done by the power of God, though perhaps by the intervention of an angel; he reports writers who say an angel came and wrote, and one who names him, but calls that conjecture. What he will fix is the timing: it appeared at the very hour when the king and his nobles were revelling, praising their idols and reproaching the God of Israel. Calvin insists it was not a man’s hand; it had the appearance of one and is therefore so called, as Scripture commonly speaks of external symbols. Clarke notices the posture, the fingers collected about the style or pen as in the act of writing; Wesley says only that it was the likeness of a hand.

Who saw what is asked by two of them. Ellicott observes that only a portion of the hand was seen by the king, that we are not told whether the guests saw it at all, and that the writing was certainly visible to all; and he remarks that in other supernatural manifestations recorded in Scripture a portion only has been witnessed by many, while the whole has been seen by one or by a few. Calvin turns the bare wall into evidence. God wrote by his own power but showed the king the figure as though a man were writing it; had the hand been on the wall from the first, he might have supposed some artifice placed it there, whereas the wall was bare and the hand suddenly appeared. He adds that the king was himself an eyewitness, that perhaps his nobles were not, and that when they saw his countenance changed they began to fear with him.

The furniture of the room tells them the hour. Calvin concludes from the lamp that this was a feast by night, and that Babylon was taken in the middle of the night; nor is he surprised the banquet ran so late, since intemperance has no bounds and men celebrating a splendid feast do not find the daylight sufficient. Ellicott takes in the same hour to mean suddenly and unexpectedly, says the candlestick would make hand and writing more distinctly visible, and notes that plaster was invariably used in the inner chambers of those palaces.

The terror is described by stages. Clarke counts five: the face grows pale, the mind is greatly agitated, pains seize the lower part of the back, a universal tremor takes place so that the knees smite together, and last comes either a swoon or the cry of distress. Gill watches the same face: the ruddy countenance and the gay airs, and all the jollity that had appeared in it, changed into paleness, sadness and confusion. Ellicott says the whole expression changed to alarm instead of drunken mirth, and Wesley draws the moral, that so soon can the terrors of God bring down the loftiest cedars, the tyrants of the earth. Keil and Delitzsch attend to the grammar: the king stands absolutely in the clause because what is to be depicted is the impression the occurrence made on him, and the plural has an intensive force, the colour of the countenance.

Calvin asks what the fear was for. The prophet describes it at length lest any think the fright groundless, and it was needful the king should be so struck, that all might understand God was seated on his throne and had summoned him as a criminal. His careless security proves his pride, for when the daily siege ought to have made him anxious he was holding his usual banquets as if in profound peace, corrupted by a kind of spiritual drunkenness so that he did not feel his own calamities; and since no ordinary means were effectual, God roused him out of his lethargy.
7:
The cry is noticed before its object. Gill says he cried with a strong voice, as loud as he could, which shows his fright and impatience, laying aside all decency and forgetting his royal majesty like a man out of his senses; this, he adds, was the usual course of the kings of Babylon in matters of difficulty, though they often found it fruitless. Calvin makes the same point: to cry out at table was beneath his dignity, but God expelled all pride from him by compelling him to burst forth like a man beside himself. Clarke says he knew it must be some awful portent.

Who was summoned, and who was not, occupies the rest. Ellicott notices that the magicians do not appear here, and supposes either that they are included under the general name or that the king in his terror forgot them; the wise men who came were the body over which Daniel was president, and he thinks it needless to ask why Daniel did not come at first. Keil and Delitzsch observe that only three classes are named as ordered in, while all the wise men are said to have come, and take it as probable that at first only those three were commanded; but they call untenable the supposition built on that, that the king chose those three on purpose to avoid Daniel, out of a heathen fear of the God of the Jews.

Calvin is harder on the omission. Daniel ought to have stood first even among the Chaldeans, for the answer he gave the grandfather of this king, foretelling he should become like the beasts of the forest, was verified by the event, and such authority ought to have flourished a thousand years; yet he was daily in the sight of the king and neglected. The native teachers were in such repute that they obscured his fame, being indignant that a captive should be preferred; but that cannot excuse a king whose own grandfather had been a memorable instance of the vengeance of God. Ellicott adds that on another view a triumvirate existed, and the promised third place was that rank.

Why the wise men failed is answered three ways. Clarke says the writing was in pure Hebrew and not the Chaldean character. Ellicott reports three conjectures, that the character was an old Semitic one they did not know, that the language was unknown to them, or that the words stood in vertical columns while they tried to read across; but the only true explanation, he holds, is the supernatural character of the inscription and the inspiration of Daniel, by which God asserts himself against the false wisdom of the heathen. Calvin knows the same guesses, that the letters were transposed, or exchanged for equivalents, or the characters altered, and calls them frivolous, since the words stood in plain order; he thinks the writing was likely visible to the king and concealed from the rest, or that they were struck blind, as a prophet threatened the law should be a sealed book to men who seemed sharper than others.

The failure doubles the fear. Gill says the king was troubled a second time and more than before, having hoped they would inform him. Ellicott traces the terror of king and lords to the impression that the failure to read the inscription was itself the portent of some terrible calamity. Keil and Delitzsch say the word means not merely consternation but confusion, a great commotion in the assembly: the magnates spoke without intelligence and the company was thrown into disorder. Calvin values the publicity, since the king was slain that very night, and so remarkable an example of justice might have been buried in a drunken revel had it not been made conspicuous; and he has no doubt Cyrus was afterwards told of it, since he would not otherwise have honoured Daniel so remarkably.
10:
Who the queen was nearly all of them canvass. Gill sets aside a writer who made her the wife of Belshazzar and takes her for the queen mother, naming her Nitocris and citing Herodotus for her prudence, though he reports another who made her the widow of Nebuchadnezzar; being an ancient woman, she was not among the ladies at the feast, but came in unsent. Clarke says it is generally allowed she was the widow of Nebuchadnezzar, but reports the other view. Keil and Delitzsch settle it by the narrative: the wives were already at the festival, and this queen comes before the king as only a mother could, the mother of a reigning king being held in high respect among the Israelites also. Wesley notes that the women of those courts had an apartment to themselves, and that she broke the rule by coming in. Calvin alone declines to choose, allowing she was probably old since she speaks of things in the time of Nebuchadnezzar, but saying the conjecture has no sufficient foundation and it is better to suspend judgment than assert anything rashly.

Her errand Henry puts as fetching a physician for the melancholy of the king. She could not read the writing, but could direct him to one who could; and Henry adds the sting, that Daniel should have been called first. Ellicott finds her respect for him evident in her language, and her position one of influence, since her advice was no sooner offered than taken.

Calvin will not let the queen excuse the king. Daniel had renown among men of all ages, and God had marked him out; that Belshazzar should be ignorant of such a prophet in his own kingdom was the fruit of gross negligence. Calvin adds that Daniel himself had no wish to be reckoned among the magi, and would have deserved to lose the prophetic spirit had he mingled with impostors; Nebuchadnezzar had set him over them all, but he never wished to exercise the honour. From this Calvin warns how prone we are to the blandishments of the world, for when a man sees a prospect of profit or honour, ambition blinds him to what he ought to do.

The word father is worked over twice. Ellicott says no blood relationship is necessarily implied, and that it means no more than predecessor. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the judgment the queen passes on Daniel is that of Nebuchadnezzar himself, and that her stating it in the same words argues that he was her husband; and they take the repeated phrase at the close of the verse as a vocative, thy father, O king, by which the words make a greater impression. Gill fastens on another phrase, that she says a man in thy kingdom and not in thy court, and infers that after the death of Nebuchadnezzar he had been removed from his offices, since otherwise she would have named one.

What was found in him is described three ways. Henry gives a full character: light and understanding and wisdom were found in him, with such insight into things secret and foresight of things to come that he was evidently inspired; and he had an admirably good heart as well as head, of a humble and heavenly spirit. Calvin sees in the three gifts she names the reason he was made master of the wise men, since the magi boasted the same abilities and their boast had twice been shown vanity; and he takes her mention of the name given him by the king as telling Belshazzar in what esteem his grandfather held the man. Gill divides the praise: the excellent spirit she meant was a superiority to all the wise men of Babylon in natural knowledge and political wisdom, but there was a more excellent spirit in him, of real grace and true piety, which she knew nothing of.
13:
The advice was taken at once. Keil and Delitzsch note that the counsel of the queen was followed without delay, and that the question, Art thou that Daniel, expects no answer but means, thou art indeed Daniel. The address shows the king knew his origin, which the queen had not mentioned, but had had no official dealings with him, and that Daniel was no longer president of the magicians. Gill supposes officers fetched him from his house in the city, since he no longer seems to have lived at court. Ellicott thinks the mention of his changed name recalled the whole circumstance to the king, and that he uses the Hebrew name to avoid one that sounded so much like his own; he adds that Daniel was by now nearly ninety.

Calvin hears contempt in the question. The king does not acknowledge his own folly but interrogates Daniel without modesty, and as a captive, to keep him in servile obedience; he had heard of the man before and said nothing, and only now, when extreme necessity urges him, does he pay him the greatest respect. Calvin says the same of the appeal to hearsay: by depending on the reports of others the king displays his slothfulness, for he ought to have known the prophet by experience, and being content with rumour he proudly neglected the teacher offered him. Gill puts it more gently, that he had probably heard of him often, though he did not think fit to use him as his grandfather had, or else had heard of him only now from the queen, whose praises he recites in her own words.

The phrase about the spirit of the gods two of them weigh. Keil and Delitzsch note, and think it not to be overlooked, that the king leaves out the word holy which the queen had used with the very same phrase. Calvin takes the plural as the common custom of the nations, which mingled angels with God promiscuously, since men in that darkness could not tell which was the true God. Yet the phrase proves, he says, that men were never so brutal as not to ascribe all excellence to God: whatever is remarkable for dignity they treat as a benefit derived from above, and so the Chaldeans called the gift of intelligence a spirit of the gods, acknowledging that no man attains such penetration by his own industry.

The failure of the wise men the king restates himself. Gill notes that they had not come of themselves nor at his cry, but were sent for and introduced by officers. Keil and Delitzsch take the word for the conjurers as standing in apposition to the wise men by way of explanation, and hold that what the king wants explained is not the writing merely as words but the writing together with its wonderful origin. Ellicott says the thing means the whole of this miraculous transaction. Clarke glosses the dissolving of doubts as untying knots, unbinding what is bound, an expression used in the east for a judge of eminent wisdom and skill.

Calvin reads the renewed offer of reward as a sign the fright had passed. God punished the king by showing how profitless were those in whom he trusted at the moment of his extremity, and in owning himself disappointed he confesses, without meaning to, that his rejection of the prophet had been intolerable; the confession is not ingenuous but violently extorted. Yet he promises Daniel the same dignity he had promised the rest, though the end of his reign was at hand, which shows how rapidly the terror had vanished. He is agitated like madmen, who, having no certainty, exult in the midst of their terror; and though he trembles at the judgment of God he keeps a hidden obstinacy, imagining his kingdom will stand while he promises wealth and honours to others.
17:
The refusal is noticed by all of them, and explained by one. Gill says he answered with great freedom and intrepidity; Clarke observes that the gifts could be of little use to anybody, since the city was within hours of being taken and pillaged; and Ellicott, noting that Daniel refused at first and afterwards accepted, takes the refusal as showing his determination to speak the truth without respect to fee, gift or reward. Calvin asks the harder question, why he did not refuse before, having rather seemed to delight in the honours conferred by Nebuchadnezzar. His answer is the difference between the two kings: in the grandfather some feelings of honour still remained, and the prophet hoped well of him, while this king had come to his last extremity and showed greater obstinacy, so that far less deference was due to him.

The purple at the end of the chapter Calvin treats as the other half of that question. Daniel does not strive vehemently against the offer, lest he be thought to act cunningly in order to escape danger. At the outset he declared the gifts valueless, knowing the end of the kingdom to be at hand; afterwards he received the purple. Had he refused it outright, Calvin says, it would have been counted a fault and a sign of timidity, and would have incurred the suspicion of treason.

Why the speech begins a generation back is answered two ways. Keil and Delitzsch take the address, Thou O king, as an absolute clause not resumed for several verses, so that everything said about Nebuchadnezzar stands in definite relation to Belshazzar; and they hold the brilliant description of that power has the undeniable object of impressing on the younger king that he did not equal his father. Calvin says Daniel did not begin the reading at once, as he conveniently might, because the king could not have profited by so abrupt a speech. The point is that it is no wonder God put forth his hand, since the king had too obstinately provoked him: his grandfather had subdued the whole world and made all men tremble at his word, and was afterwards hurled from the throne, so that Belshazzar had a signal example before him, and when that domestic admonition did not profit him the time was ripe for a portentous sign.

What the majesty was for Calvin makes the doctrine of the passage. Empires are bestowed by divine power and not by chance, and God wishes his power to be specially visible in kingdoms; though he takes care of the whole world and regulates even the most miserable things, his singular providence shines out in the empire of the world. By the words that follow, Calvin says, the glory of God is inscribed on kings, although he allows them to reign supreme: they are divinely armed with authority and so hold a great multitude under their sway. He asks how, since ambition is natural to every man, it comes about that many thousands are subject to one and endure many oppressions from him. Gill takes the majesty for the greatness of his power, the largeness of his dominions and the vast armies at his command, and Clarke reads the power of life and death that follows as the genuine character of a despot, whose will is the only rule of his conduct.

Henry states the doom in a sentence and then applies it. The king had not taken warning by the judgments upon Nebuchadnezzar, and he had insulted God; sinners are pleased with gods that neither see nor hear nor know, but they will be judged by one to whom all things are open. The application Henry makes general: at death the days of a sinner are numbered and finished, after death comes the judgment in which he is weighed and found wanting.
20:
The fall of the grandfather is told again as a warning. Gill traces the pride to the successes and victories, the enlarged dominions and the glory he had arrived at; the word, he notes, may be rendered to deal proudly, or to do wickedly, since pride puts great men upon things extremely vile. Clarke says he was deposed, became insane, and the reins of government were taken from his hands. Gill describes the madness as of a kind that made him choose the company of beasts rather than of men, or else as so intolerable that his courtiers were obliged to remove him from palace and court; Ellicott notes that the dwelling among wild asses is a detail supplementary to the earlier chapter.

Calvin works over the wording before he draws the lesson. The verb is literally put, so that some translate that the king placed his own heart among the brutes, assimilating his senses to theirs, while others refer it to God, who placed his heart among the beasts and so infatuated him as to render him like them. On the next clause some render that he was made to taste the grass like a brute and others that the grass supported him; Calvin finds no doubt about the sense. The point is that he was deprived of reason and judgment, the principal difference between men and brutes; and the man who had dwelt in a palace conspicuous to the world, from whom all the people of the East sought their laws, and who was habitually worshipped as a god, afterwards dwelt among wild beasts. It was an example worth handing down to a thousand generations, had the monarchy lasted so long, and the grandson quickly forgot it.

The charge turns on that forgetting. Clarke says judgments and mercies alike had no good effect on him. Ellicott says the whole history was known to him, but he had not learned its moral lesson, and was doubly guilty, since his blasphemy was wilful. Calvin says the king ought to have been so affected by a domestic example as to submit himself to God, and that the circumstance presses on him the duty of not seeking an instance among foreign nations when he had one at home. Men shield themselves under ignorance to extenuate their crimes, but those who sin knowingly are without the slightest excuse, so the prophet convicts him of manifest obstinacy, as one who provoked the anger of God on purpose.

The lifting up is measured against its object. Gill says it is the Lord of heaven who made it and dwells in it, and thence beholds all the actions of men; the words may even be rendered above the Lord of heaven, which shows the pride of the king and his ignorance both of himself and of the true God. Clarke finds the highest evidence of the rebellion in the profaning of the sacred vessels. Calvin says that had the king raised himself so insolently against men his sin would have deserved punishment, but when he provoked God on purpose the arrogance could not be borne; the profanation was sacrilege, and he was not content with that indignity but used the vessels for luxury in the company of abandoned women.

The last clause names what he owed. Calvin points to the God on whom he depended and from whom all he boasted of proceeded, so that to despise a living God who had been so gracious was base ingratitude; and he observes that Daniel here sustains the character of a teacher, where at the start of the chapter he spoke as a historian. Ellicott adds a limit the king had overrun: the Israelites were his subjects by right of conquest, but their God was not his to blaspheme, and Scripture has other instances of men exceeding their authority while acting as ministers of the chastisement of God.
24:
Where the hand came from is settled first. Gill says it was from God, sent at that instant and for that reason, because the vessels of his sanctuary were profaned and idol gods praised while he was despised; Wesley puts it in five words, from that God whom thou hast despised. Ellicott notes that the opening word means not only at that time but because of this, and that Daniel expressly designates the writing as proceeding from God. Clarke calls the moment the filling up of the cup of iniquity, the act that made the king ripe for destruction.

Calvin weighs the same adverb. The wrath, or at least its denunciation, was now ripe, and the prophet shows how patiently God had borne with the king; but he now comes forth as a judge and ascends his judgment seat, since the haughtiness was desperate and the impiety no longer tolerable. Thou canst not complain of the swiftness of the penalty, Calvin has him told, as though God had exacted it before the time; consider rather how long thou hast provoked him. Nor need the king inquire where the hand came from: it is a witness of the wrath of heaven, not a spectre that will vanish, but a proof of divine displeasure.

Why the Chaldeans could not read it Clarke answers from the alphabet. Had the words stood in the Chaldean character, every man present who could read his own alphabet could have read them; but the character now called Hebrew is in fact the Chaldean, while the true Hebrew is the one now called Samaritan, which the Jews used before the captivity, so that Daniel could read it easily and the wise men of Babylon could not. It was simply the strangeness of the character, Clarke concludes, the two differing in ancient times more than they now appear to. Calvin will have none of it: the king could not read either through stupor or because God blunted his senses and blinded his eyes, and the same must be said of the magi, who could have read had they not been struck blind.

The words are then taken apart. Clarke observes that each stands for a short sentence, numbering, weighing and division, and that all the ancient versions but one give the words simply, without the repetition of the first and without the conjunction on the last. Ellicott remarks that the word occurring twice in the inscription appears only once in the interpretation, while the Medes named in the interpretation are not named in the inscription; hence the conjecture that the second occurrence was originally the name of Media, which he calls plausible but without external support. He takes the repetition for emphasis, and notes that the first word carries both numbering and bringing to an end, the second both the act of weighing and the fact of being found light, while the last begins with the conjunction and continues with a plural that carries both divisions and Persians.

Calvin reads the doubling as confirmation. Some conjecture it applies to the years of the life of the king and also of his reign, but the guess seems to him groundless; he thinks the word is used twice because men allow calculations to be liable to error, so that God affirms the number complete and not a moment to be added to the boundary already fixed. From this Calvin draws a general instruction, that God has prescribed a certain time for all kingdoms as Scripture says he has for the life of each of us; and if he has fixed the length of a man’s life, the rule holds the more forcibly of empires. There is consolation in it, he says, when we see tyrants rushing on without moderation, as though they would mingle heaven and earth: their years are numbered, and God knows how long they are to rage.
26:
The interpretation is given word by word. Gill notes that the whole may be called one word, since the four might seem as one; and Wesley renders the first, it is numbered, it is numbered, saying the doubling is for greater confirmation and relates to the seventy years appointed for the overthrow of the Babylonish empire.

On the second word Calvin dwells on the figure. Daniel shows God so moderating his judgments as if he carried a balance in his hand, an emblem taken from the custom of men; so God is said to treat all things by weight and measure, since he does nothing in confusion, and nothing under his hand is more or less than it should be. He did not hasten to punish but exacted it justly, by his own uniform rule. To be found wanting is to be found light and without weight, and Calvin puts the sentence directly: thou thinkest thy dignity must be spared, since all men revere thee; but God judges otherwise, and does not use a common scale but holds his own. He adds that the tyrant was without doubt greatly exasperated, and that God restrained him from rising up against the prophet.

The third word carries two things at once. Wesley says it means separated, divided, broken, and signifies both that the kingdom was broken off from Belshazzar and that it was given to the Persians; Gill notes that the form here is the singular of the plural used in the writing. Calvin takes it of the instability of the monarchy, which God wished utterly to abolish, but finds in it an apt allusion to the division between the two nations, so that the disgrace of Babylon lay in serving many masters. It is disgrace enough when a people that has held a wide empire is subjected to one master; under two the indignity is greater. Yet Calvin holds there was properly no division at all: the city was taken by the valour of Cyrus, who then admitted his father-in-law to share the royal authority, and on that account the Medes and Persians are said to have divided the kingdom.

The reward is paid at once. Keil and Delitzsch note that the king fulfilled his promise, and are careful about the verb: it does not say he commanded them to clothe Daniel, which would require another form, but that they clothed him, so that the command was carried out and he was adorned with purple and a golden chain and proclaimed third ruler of the kingdom. They know the objection that such a dignity was impossible, since the king was slain that night, and answer that it rests on a supposition about how the proclamation was made. Clarke says the word rendered scarlet more probably means purple, and that the gold chain was an emblem of magisterial authority, often so mentioned in Scripture.

Why he kept his word is answered two ways. Gill supposes that instead of being full of wrath he gave the reward to show a regard to his word and honour as a king and to secure his credit with his nobles; or that he did not gather how near the destruction was, or put the evil day far from him. Calvin finds the order surprising in a man so sharply reproved, and knows those who explain it by the binding force of a royal word among the Babylonians. His own opinion is that the king was consulting his own ease and safety, since otherwise he would have been contemptible to his nobles: to show himself unmoved he has Daniel robed, as though the threat had been harmless. He did not despise what the prophet said, but wished to persuade his nobles and guests of his indifference; for kings, when greatly terrified, are careful to show no sign of timidity, thinking their authority would be weakened by it.
30:
How the king died they take from the historians. Gill sets aside the accounts that make it a servant of his own or a eunuch of the guard, and follows the story of two officers who led the army up the bed of the river, its course turned; the inhabitants were revelling and the gates open, and the palace doors were opened by the king himself to learn what the noise was, so that they rushed in and slew him standing with his sword drawn. Clarke tells it the same way, of two lords who had gone over to the conqueror to avenge wrongs done them, and notes that the city was entered by the bed of the Euphrates, emptied by a channel that turned the waters into the marshes. Henry keeps to the moral: in that night, when his heart was merry with wine, the besiegers broke in and made for the palace, and no place was secret enough to conceal him nor strong enough to protect him; death comes as a snare on those whose hearts are overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness.

Calvin rejects one version of the story. He will not have it that a guard stabbed the king on hearing the voice of the prophet and wishing to execute that judgment, as if the sentence of God depended on the will of a single heathen; the truth is that the king was seized in his own banqueting room, grossly intoxicated, among his nobles and concubines. Calvin turns to the escape of Daniel, and calls it a wonderful kindness of God: he stood in no danger, though clad in purple, and scarcely an hour passed before the Medes and Persians were in the city, so that he could hardly have escaped unless God had covered him with the shadow of his hand. He was much agitated, no doubt, for he was not without feeling; but he was to be so exercised, that he might acknowledge God the faithful guardian of his life.

How long the reign had run Gill takes from the chronologies, seventeen years by the reckoning he prefers, against a Jewish chronicle that allows three because no more are named in Scripture. Keil and Delitzsch mark the moment differently: with the death of the king that night the interpretation began to be fulfilled, and that beginning gave certainty that the rest would also be accomplished.

Who Darius the Median was is the last question. Gill and Clarke identify him with Cyaxares, son of Astyages and uncle of Cyrus, called the Median to distinguish him from a later king of the name; Gill says he took Babylon from the conqueror with his consent, being the senior prince, and reigned two years, and not alone. Wesley says only that this was he who with Cyrus took Babylon.

Calvin and Ellicott are the least confident. Calvin grants that Babylon was taken under the auspices of Cyrus, though he is not named here, and explains the silence by the honour due to a father-in-law, the conqueror being content with the fame of the victory and readily conceding the title to an old man he saw growing infirm. Whether he was the son of Astyages he leaves undecided, passing over the stories told about the birth of Cyrus as uncertain. Ellicott takes the verb to mean that he received the kingdom from the hands of a conqueror, and admits plainly that this Darius cannot be identified with any person in profane history and that no trace of the name is found in the inscriptions of the period; he rests the case on the accuracy of the book elsewhere. Henry makes the transfer the point: from the head of gold we descend to the breast and arms of silver, and notice is taken of the age of the new king, for which his nephew gave him precedency.
